data.title: Squamous cell carcinoma — viva
data.summary: Premalignant & malignant tumours · 28 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Squamous cell carcinoma** (Premalignant & malignant tumours)_

**Q1. Define cutaneous SCC (cSCC).**
- Malignant tumour of epidermal keratinocytes with invasion into the dermis, capable of local destruction and metastasis (2–5% overall; higher in high-risk tumours); second commonest skin cancer worldwide; in India often arises on chronic scars/ulcers and in genital or oral mucosa

**Q2. Describe SCC: types and risk factors (PYQ).**
- Risk factors: cumulative UV exposure, fair skin, age, chronic immunosuppression (organ transplant — 65–250× risk; azathioprine, voriconazole), HPV (periungual/genital — 16, 18; β-HPV in EDV), ionising radiation, arsenic, tar, mineral oils, PUVA, smoking (lip), chronic inflammation and scars (burns — Marjolin's ulcer, lupus vulgaris, DLE, chronic ulcers, osteomyelitis sinus, lichen sclerosus, erosive LP, DEB, HS), Kangri cancer (Kashmir — abdominal wall from fire pot), Kang cancer, dhoti cancer (waist), chutta cancer (reverse smoking — palate), betel/tobacco chewing (oral), xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism, BRAF inhibitors (keratoacanthoma-like)
- Precursors: actinic keratosis, Bowen's disease (SCC in situ), actinic cheilitis, leukoplakia/erythroplakia, erythroplasia of Queyrat (glans), bowenoid papulosis, arsenical keratoses, porokeratosis

**Q3. Clinical types.**
- In situ: Bowen's disease — slowly enlarging, well-defined, red scaly plaque (lower legs of elderly women, trunk); erythroplasia of Queyrat (velvety red plaque on glans of uncircumcised men)
- Invasive: indurated keratotic nodule or plaque, ulcer with raised everted indurated edges, cutaneous horn, verrucous/exophytic, bleeding; sun-exposed sites (ear, lip, scalp, dorsum of hand) or on scars
- Variants: keratoacanthoma (well-differentiated SCC variant — rapidly growing crateriform nodule with central keratin plug in weeks, may regress), verrucous carcinoma (low-grade — oral florid papillomatosis, Buschke–Löwenstein (genital), epithelioma cuniculatum (plantar)), spindle-cell, acantholytic, adenosquamous, desmoplastic (aggressive)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Irregular nests and strands of atypical squamous cells invading the dermis from the epidermis, keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, dyskeratosis, mitoses
- Broders' grading by differentiation: well (>75% differentiated), moderately, poorly (<25%), undifferentiated
- Keratoacanthoma: symmetric cup-shaped crater filled with keratin, glassy eosinophilic cells, buttresses ('lipping') at edges

**Q5. High-risk features.**
- Diameter ≥2 cm, depth >6 mm or beyond subcutaneous fat, poor differentiation, perineural invasion (nerve ≥0.1 mm), desmoplastic/acantholytic subtype, location — ear, lip, temple, H-zone, genital; arising in scar/chronic ulcer or radiation site; immunosuppression; recurrent tumour; rapid growth
- Staging: AJCC 8th (head and neck) and Brigham and Women's Hospital (T1–T3 by risk factors)

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Keratoacanthoma, BCC, AK (hypertrophic), wart, seborrhoeic keratosis (irritated), amelanotic melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, prurigo nodule, chronic infections (TBVC, chromoblastomycosis, deep fungal, mycetoma, leishmaniasis — pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia mimics SCC)

**Q7. Investigations.**
- Biopsy (incisional/excisional) including deep tissue; examine regional lymph nodes; FNAC/USG of nodes; CT/MRI for deep invasion, perineural spread or nodal disease; sentinel lymph node biopsy (selected high-risk)

**Q8. Management.**
- Low-risk: surgical excision with 4–6 mm margins; curettage and electrodesiccation for small low-risk; cryotherapy for in situ
- High-risk: wide excision with ≥6 mm margins or Mohs surgery; adjuvant radiotherapy for perineural invasion/positive margins/nodal disease; nodal dissection for nodal metastasis
- Bowen's disease: 5-FU, imiquimod, PDT, cryotherapy, curettage, excision
- Advanced/metastatic or unresectable: immune checkpoint inhibitors — cemiplimab (first approved), pembrolizumab; EGFR inhibitor cetuximab; platinum chemotherapy (older)
- Prevention: sun protection, treat precursors, nicotinamide, acitretin in transplant recipients, switch immunosuppressant to sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor)
- Follow-up: 3–6 monthly for 2 years then yearly; skin and node examination

**Q9. Discuss cutaneous markers of internal malignancy (PYQ).**
- Paraneoplastic dermatoses: acanthosis nigricans (malignant), tripe palms, Leser–Trélat sign, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica of Bazex (SCC upper aerodigestive tract), erythema gyratum repens (lung), necrolytic migratory erythema (glucagonoma), hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita, dermatomyositis, paraneoplastic pemphigus, Sweet syndrome/pyoderma gangrenosum (haematological), Trousseau's migratory thrombophlebitis (pancreas), carcinoid flushing, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, pachydermoperiostosis, ichthyosis acquisita (lymphoma), extramammary Paget's
- Genetic syndromes with skin markers: Gardner, Muir–Torre (sebaceous tumours), Cowden (trichilemmomas), Peutz–Jeghers, Birt–Hogg–Dubé, Gorlin, MEN 2B (mucosal neuromas), Howel–Evans, Carney complex

**Q10. Describe precursor lesions of SCC.**
- Actinic keratosis (most common precursor), Bowen's disease (SCC in situ), actinic cheilitis (lower lip), erythroplasia of Queyrat (glans), leukoplakia/ erythroplakia (oral), bowenoid papulosis, arsenical keratoses, chronic radiation dermatitis, chronic scars/ ulcers (Marjolin), porokeratosis, LS, erosive LP, HPV-related warts in immunosuppressed

**Q11. What is Bowen's disease and its management?**
- Intraepidermal SCC (full-thickness atypia): slowly enlarging, well-demarcated, red scaly plaque on sun-exposed skin (legs of elderly women), or trunk (arsenic); ~3–5% progress to invasive SCC
- Treatment: 5-FU, imiquimod, PDT (excellent for large/leg lesions with poor healing), cryotherapy, curettage, excision; erythroplasia of Queyrat — glans (higher progression)

**Q12. What is keratoacanthoma?**
- Rapidly growing (weeks) dome-shaped nodule with central keratin-filled crater on sun-exposed skin of elderly; may involute spontaneously in months leaving scar; considered a well-differentiated SCC variant — treat as SCC (excision); multiple KAs — Ferguson-Smith (TGFBR1), Grzybowski (eruptive), Muir–Torre; drug-induced (BRAF inhibitors — vemurafenib)

**Q13. Describe the TNM staging principles of cSCC (AJCC 8th, head and neck).**
- T1 <2 cm; T2 2–4 cm; T3 >4 cm or minor bone erosion, perineural invasion, or deep invasion (beyond subcutaneous fat or >6 mm); T4 gross bone/skull base invasion
- N staging by node size/number/extranodal extension; M1 distant metastasis
- Brigham and Women's Hospital (BWH) staging uses high-risk factors (≥2 cm, poorly differentiated, perineural invasion of nerve ≥0.1 mm, invasion beyond fat) — better prognostic discrimination

**Q14. Which areas carry higher metastatic risk?**
- Lip and ear (mucocutaneous junctions), temple, scalp, genitals (penile/vulval), SCC arising in chronic scars/ulcers (Marjolin) or radiation sites, perineural invasion, immunosuppressed patients — metastasis rates 10–30% vs ~2–5% overall

**Q15. Surgical management and margins.**
- Low-risk SCC: excision with 4–6 mm clinical margins; high-risk: ≥6–10 mm margins or Mohs micrographic surgery (complete margin control); assess regional nodes clinically/ ultrasound; sentinel lymph node biopsy in selected high-risk tumours
- Adjuvant radiotherapy for perineural invasion, close/positive margins, nodal disease with extracapsular extension

**Q16. Systemic treatment of advanced SCC.**
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1) — cemiplimab (first-line for locally advanced/ metastatic cSCC — response ~45–50%), pembrolizumab; cetuximab (EGFR) for those unfit for immunotherapy; platinum chemotherapy older option; transplant recipients — reduce immunosuppression, switch to sirolimus (mTOR inhibitors have anti-tumour effect)

**Q17. SCC in organ transplant recipients — why and how to manage?**
- Immunosuppression (azathioprine, calcineurin inhibitors) + UV + HPV → SCC 65–250× higher, more aggressive, multiple, SCC:BCC ratio reversed (~4:1)
- Management: strict sun protection, regular skin checks (3–12 monthly), early treatment of AKs (field therapy), nicotinamide, acitretin chemoprevention (10–25 mg/day), reduce/switch immunosuppression (sirolimus/everolimus)

**Q18. Penile and vulval SCC — risk factors.**
- Penile: phimosis, poor hygiene, uncircumcised, HPV 16/18, lichen sclerosus (BXO), smoking, PUVA; presents as ulcer/ growth on glans/ prepuce; inguinal nodes
- Vulval: HPV-related (younger — usual VIN) and HPV-independent (older — LS/differentiated VIN, p53 mutation); itchy lump/ ulcer

**Q19. Oral SCC and its premalignant lesions in India.**
- High burden due to tobacco chewing (gutka, khaini), betel quid, smoking, alcohol; premalignant — leukoplakia (white plaque not rubbed off), erythroplakia (highest risk), oral submucous fibrosis (areca nut — trismus, blanching), erosive LP; buccal mucosa commonest site in India; biopsy persistent lesions >2 weeks

**Q20. Verrucous carcinoma — what is it?**
- Well-differentiated low-grade SCC variant — slow-growing exophytic cauliflower-like mass with 'pushing' borders; sites — oral (oral florid papillomatosis), anogenital (Buschke–Löwenstein), plantar (epithelioma cuniculatum — sinus tracts like rabbit burrows); rarely metastasises; wide excision (radiotherapy may cause anaplastic transformation)

**Q21. Histological grading (Broders).**
- Grade 1: >75% differentiated (keratin pearls, intercellular bridges); 2: 50–75%; 3: 25–50%; 4: <25% (poorly differentiated, spindle cell)
- Variants: acantholytic, spindle cell (sarcomatoid — cytokeratin+), desmoplastic (high-risk), adenosquamous, clear cell

**Q22. Differentiate keratoacanthoma from SCC clinically and histologically.**
- KA: rapid growth over weeks, symmetrical crateriform with central keratin plug, may regress; histology — symmetrical cup-shaped architecture with 'lipping' buttresses, glassy eosinophilic keratinocytes, intraepithelial neutrophilic microabscesses
- SCC: slower, irregular, ulcerated, infiltrative strands with atypia; often impossible to separate — treat KA as SCC

**Q23. Prevention and chemoprevention.**
- Sun protection (sunscreens reduce SCC — Nambour trial), avoid tanning, treat AK, nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily, acitretin in transplant recipients and XP, HPV vaccination (anogenital), stop tobacco/areca nut (oral), avoid arsenic-contaminated water

**Q24. What is Marjolin's ulcer?**
- SCC arising in chronic scars (burns commonest), chronic osteomyelitis sinuses, venous ulcers, pressure sores, lupus vulgaris, DLE, hidradenitis; long latency (decades); aggressive with high nodal metastasis — biopsy any non-healing ulcer with raised edge/ growth

**Q25. Examination of a patient with suspected SCC — what do you check?**
- Lesion: size, site, edge (raised/ everted), base, induration, fixation to deeper structures, bleeding, perineural symptoms (pain, numbness, facial weakness)
- Regional lymph nodes (parotid, cervical, axillary, inguinal), whole-skin exam for other cancers/ AKs, oral cavity, immune status

**Q26. Prognosis.**
- Overall 5-year cure >90% for primary low-risk SCC after excision; recurrent, perineural, poorly differentiated, immunosuppressed and nodal disease have worse outcome (nodal metastasis 5-year survival ~50%)

**Q27. Cutaneous markers of internal malignancy (expanded).**
- Paraneoplastic dermatoses: acanthosis nigricans (malignant), tripe palms, Leser–Trélat sign, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica of Bazex (upper aerodigestive SCC), erythema gyratum repens (lung), necrolytic migratory erythema (glucagonoma), hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita, dermatomyositis, paraneoplastic pemphigus, Sweet syndrome (AML), pyoderma gangrenosum (myeloma), Trousseau sign (migratory thrombophlebitis — pancreatic), carcinoid flushing, Sister Mary Joseph nodule (umbilical metastasis), extramammary Paget's, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, pachydermoperiostosis/ clubbing (lung)

**Q28. Bazex syndrome — explain.**
- Acrokeratosis paraneoplastica: psoriasiform violaceous scaly plaques on ears, nose, fingers/ toes and nails (acral) in men >40 with SCC of upper aerodigestive tract (pharynx, larynx, oesophagus) or lung; improves with tumour treatment

## Quick spotter facts
- Ulcer with raised everted indurated edge on old burn scar — Marjolin's SCC
- Keratin pearls, Broders' grading
- Kangri cancer — Kashmir

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Squamous cell carcinoma; keratoacanthoma); Brigham and Women's / AJCC staging concepts. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
